水琴常見於電影配樂、電視製作、唱片與現場演出，也進入交響樂團、巡迴樂團與錄音室。: The waterphone is common in film scores, television production, records and live performance, and has entered symphony orchestras, touring bands and recording studios. It appears in works such as Howard Goodall's musical The Dreaming, Derek Bourgeois's Symphony No. 59, Tan Dun's opera The First Emperor, Jean-Michel Jarre's album Oxymore and the rock album Feast; it has also been played underwater, and used to call whales and dolphins.
水琴為北美體鳴樂器（Hornbostel–Sachs 13），演奏時多採坐姿。一: The waterphone is a North American idiophone (Hornbostel–Sachs 13), usually played seated. One hand holds the nylon cord at the top of the resonating chamber, the other holds a violin bow or a rubber ball mallet; the player bows or strikes the resonating plate and the rods while rocking the body so that the small amount of liquid inside is set moving, letting the plate, the rods and the sound of the water overlap. A beginner can start with a small amount of water, steady the grip on the nylon cord, then practise the contact point of the bow or mallet, and finally add the rocking, listening to the changes in sound the moving water makes.
水琴為體鳴樂器，美洲／北美地區使用。琴身以不鏽鋼製成共鳴碗或盤，並有圓柱頸；邊緣: The waterphone is an idiophone used in the Americas / North America. Its body is a stainless-steel resonating bowl or plate with a cylindrical neck; around the rim are sounding rods of different lengths and thicknesses, called bronze rods in the English source and steel rods in the Chinese. The resonating chamber can hold a small amount of water, and a nylon cord at the top is there to hold. It is played by rubbing or striking with an ordinary violin bow or a rubber ball, but the materials of the bow and the ball are not stated.
水琴由美國理查德·沃特斯於1968年至1969年間發明，1973年申請專利、19: The waterphone was invented by Richard Waters of the United States between 1968 and 1969; he applied for a patent in 1973 and it was granted in 1975. The idea was influenced by the Tibetan drum and is also related to the nailed piano. Four sizes were later developed, and a two-chamber waterphone appeared. The waterphone has entered museums, documentaries, symphony orchestras, recording studios and film and television scores, and has been used in rock recordings and in experiments in communication between species.
水琴的音色飄渺神秘，具有明亮而又帶有幽冷的特質。其聲響空靈詭異，帶有明顯的非諧和: The waterphone's timbre is ethereal and mysterious, bright and at the same time cold. Its sound is unearthly and strange, with a marked inharmonicity, its range wide and its pitch hard to define precisely. When the bronze rods are struck the sound rings and resonates in the stainless-steel bowl, and the water inside adds a sense of movement and a wet texture, so that the sound is layered and fluid. Its resonance is unusual, its timbre lying between bell instruments and ambient sound, with both the cold clarity of metal and the organic feel of natural water. Compared with the warm woodiness of the marimba it is stranger; compared with the crispness of the glockenspiel it is softer and more blurred, and it often creates a surreal soundscape.

The waterphone (also called the ocean harp) is a modern idiophone, Hornbostel–Sachs 13. It is a stainless-steel resonating bowl or pot with a cylindrical neck, bronze rods of different lengths and diameters around the rim, and a small amount of water in the resonating chamber. The player usually performs seated and alone, holding the nylon cord in one hand and bowing or striking with a violin bow, a superball mallet or a drumstick in the other, while rocking it so that the water moves, combining the resonance of the bowl, the rods and the water. It was invented, developed and made by the American Richard Waters, and is used in film scores, records, live performance, symphony orchestras, touring bands and studios, as well as in horror film and television and games.
